Summary: The first commandment: God alone is to be worshipped, and nothing else may rival him.
Commandment: Worship God alone; put nothing else in his place.
Application: Jesus restates this as the first and greatest commandment (Matthew 22:37-38). Idolatry today is not only statues: anything that takes God's rightful first place — wealth, status, pleasure, self — rivals him.

Summary: The second commandment: God's people must not make or worship carved images or any likeness as a god.
Commandment: Do not make or worship an idol or any image as a god.
Application: God cannot be captured in an image made by human hands. The New Testament extends the warning inward: covetousness itself is idolatry (Colossians 3:5).

Summary: The third commandment: God's name must be treated with reverence, never used emptily, falsely, or as a cover for wrongdoing.
Commandment: Do not use God's name in a worthless, false, or irreverent way.
Application: Bearing God's name is about more than speech: his people carry his name before the world, so their words and conduct must match it.

Summary: The fourth commandment: one day in seven is set apart for rest and worship, rooted in creation and in Israel's deliverance from Egypt.
Commandment: Keep one day in seven holy: rest from ordinary work and set it apart for God.
Application: Jesus calls himself Lord of the Sabbath and teaches that the Sabbath was made for people, not people for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27-28). Christians differ on whether seventh-day observance continues literally or is fulfilled in the rest Christ gives (Hebrews 4:9-10); both readings are honestly held.

Summary: The fifth commandment: parents are to be honored in word, care, and provision — the first commandment with a promise attached.
Commandment: Honor your father and mother in how you speak of them, care for them, and provide for them.
Application: Paul quotes this commandment to believers and repeats its promise: that it may go well with you and that you may live long. Honor does not end when a child leaves home; it grows into caring for aging parents.

Summary: The sixth commandment: human life, made in God's image, must not be taken unlawfully.
Commandment: Do not take a human life unlawfully.
Application: Jesus presses the commandment to the heart: contempt and hatred already break it in spirit. The commandment forbids murder, not lawful judgment or defense, which Scripture treats separately.

Summary: The seventh commandment: marriage is exclusive, and sexual faithfulness guards the covenant between husband and wife.
Commandment: Do not be unfaithful to your marriage; keep sexual union within marriage alone.
Application: Jesus extends the commandment to the heart: lustful intent already breaks it. The positive side is faithfulness that protects both spouse and family.

Summary: The eighth commandment: what belongs to another must not be taken by force, fraud, or stealth.
Commandment: Do not take what belongs to someone else.
Application: Paul turns the commandment positive: the thief must steal no longer, but work honestly and share with those in need. Theft includes fraud and withheld wages, not only burglary.

Summary: The ninth commandment: truth must be told, especially where another person's name and standing are at stake.
Commandment: Do not testify falsely against another person.
Application: False witness destroys a neighbor's reputation and corrupts justice. Jesus contrasts truth-telling with the devil, whom he calls the father of lies.

Summary: The tenth commandment: desire itself is addressed — not only acts, but the grasping heart that wants what belongs to another.
Commandment: Do not set your heart on possessing what belongs to your neighbor.
Application: This is the commandment that reaches inward, which is why Paul calls covetousness idolatry. It exposes that sin begins in desire before it becomes action.

Summary: The Shema's great demand: love for God that engages heart, soul, and strength — the whole person, not part of them.
Commandment: Love the LORD your God with all your heart, soul, and strength.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as moral. Jesus quotes this as the first and greatest commandment, and joins it to love of neighbor as the summary of the whole Law and the Prophets.

Summary: The neighbor-love law: the same care you naturally take for your own interests must extend to the person next to you.
Commandment: Love your neighbor as you love yourself; do not hate, take vengeance, or bear grudges.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as moral. Jesus pairs this with love of God as the hinge of the Law, and his parable of the Good Samaritan widens 'neighbor' beyond tribe and party.

Command: Care for the Poor, Widow, Orphan, and Stranger
Summary: A cluster of laws protecting the vulnerable: gleaning left in the fields, prompt justice, and no oppression of those without a defender.
Commandment: Leave provision for the poor and the stranger, and do not oppress the widow, the orphan, or the foreigner.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as moral. James carries the same duty into the church as pure religion: visiting orphans and widows in their affliction (James 1:27).

Summary: The marketplace law: scales, weights, and measures must be true, because fraud in trade is theft disguised as business.
Commandment: Use honest scales, weights, and measures; do not keep a double standard, one for buying and one for selling.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as moral. Proverbs repeats the principle as wisdom: a false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight delights him.

Summary: The labor law: wages must be paid promptly and workers must not be oppressed, especially the poor laborer who depends on the day's pay.
Commandment: Pay a hired worker on the day he earns it; do not hold back wages or oppress the laborer.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as moral. James warns employers directly: withheld wages cry out against them. The principle outlives the agrarian setting — honest pay, promptly given.

Summary: The holiness code's sexual laws: forbidden unions and practices that marked Israel as distinct from the surrounding nations.
Commandment: Keep sexual relations within the bounds God sets; do not practice the forbidden unions named in the Law.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as moral. The New Testament reaffirms sexual purity for believers, grounding it in the body as the temple of the Holy Spirit and in marriage as honorable.

Summary: The respect law: rise before gray hair and honor the aged, treating age itself as worthy of deference.
Commandment: Stand up in the presence of gray hair and honor the aged.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as moral. Paul applies the same posture inside the church: treat older men as fathers and older women as mothers, correcting with gentleness.

Summary: The sacrificial system: burnt, grain, peace, sin, and guilt offerings, daily, weekly, and at the appointed feasts.
Commandment: Bring the appointed offerings at the appointed times, as the Law prescribes, for atonement, thanksgiving, and fellowship with God.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Hebrews teaches these sacrifices could never perfect the worshiper; they pointed forward to Christ's once-for-all offering, which is why they ceased with the new covenant.

Summary: The annual fast and cleansing: on the tenth day of the seventh month the high priest entered the Most Holy Place with blood for the sins of the people.
Commandment: On the Day of Atonement, afflict yourselves, do no work, and let the high priest make atonement for the people.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Hebrews reads the Day as a shadow: Christ entered the true Most Holy Place with his own blood, securing an eternal redemption the yearly rite could only picture. (Distinct from the Jewish Cultural Backgrounds entry on the Day of Atonement as a feast; this entry covers the commanded rite as law.)

Summary: The dietary laws: which creatures may be eaten and which are unclean, marking Israel's table as distinct.
Commandment: Eat only what the Law calls clean; abstain from what it calls unclean.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The New Testament records these food distinctions set aside: Jesus declares all foods clean, and Peter's vision confirms that God has cleansed what was formerly called common.

Command: Purity Laws: Skin Disease, Discharges, Childbirth
Summary: The bodily purity laws: conditions that made a person ceremonially unclean and the washings and offerings that restored them.
Commandment: Follow the washings and offerings prescribed for skin disease, bodily discharges, and childbirth before returning to worship.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Jesus repeatedly touches those the purity laws isolated — the leper, the bleeding woman — and restores them, showing mercy reaching where ritual could only separate.

Summary: The commanded festival calendar: Passover, Unleavened Bread, Firstfruits, Weeks, Trumpets, Atonement, and Tabernacles, each at its appointed season.
Commandment: Observe the LORD's appointed feasts at their appointed times, with the offerings and rest each feast requires.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Paul calls Christ our Passover lamb, sacrificed for us — the feasts' meaning gathers around him. (Jewish Cultural Backgrounds covers the individual feasts as cultural background; this entry covers the commanded observance as law.)

Summary: The ordained service: the tabernacle's pattern, the priestly garments and consecration, and the priests' daily work before God.
Commandment: Build the tabernacle to the pattern shown on the mountain, and let the consecrated priests serve in it as the Law directs.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Hebrews teaches the earthly tabernacle was a copy of the heavenly one, and Christ now serves as high priest in the true tabernacle.

Summary: The giving laws: a tenth of produce and livestock for the Levites and the poor, plus firstfruits and freewill offerings.
Commandment: Give a tenth of your produce and livestock as the Law directs, and bring firstfruits and offerings to the LORD.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The New Testament shifts the frame from a fixed percentage to cheerful, generous giving — God loves a cheerful giver — while keeping the duty to support ministry and the poor.

Summary: The asylum law: six cities where a person who killed unintentionally could flee and stand trial, safe from the avenger of blood.
Commandment: Let the one who kills unintentionally flee to a city of refuge and stand trial before the congregation.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as civil. The cities balanced two truths: life is sacred, and intent matters. They protected the innocent from vengeance while still requiring a fair hearing.

Summary: The property laws: theft, damage, negligence, and lost property, with restitution scaled to the wrong.
Commandment: Repay what you stole or damaged, restore a neighbor's lost property, and make restitution as the Law scales it.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as civil. Zacchaeus shows the spirit of restitution alive in the gospel: he repaid fourfold those he had defrauded. Justice restores, not merely punishes.

Command: Debt Release, Sabbatical, and Jubilee Years
Summary: The economic reset laws: every seventh year debts released and the land rested; every fiftieth year land returned and slaves freed.
Commandment: Every seventh year release debts and let the land rest; every fiftieth year proclaim liberty and return each family to its land.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as civil. Jesus opens his ministry proclaiming release to the captives, taking up Jubilee's language for his own mission. The laws guarded against permanent destitution and permanent debt.

Summary: The land laws: inheritance passes within the family and tribe, daughters inherit when there is no son, and the land itself stays in the family.
Commandment: Keep inheritance within the tribe, let daughters inherit where there is no son, and do not sell the family's land permanently.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as civil. The daughters of Zelophehad set the precedent: their appeal changed the law itself, showing God's law making room for justice within its own framework.

Summary: The judicial laws: judges in every town, no bribes, no partiality, conviction only on two or three witnesses, and false witnesses bearing the penalty they sought.
Commandment: Appoint honest judges, take no bribe, show no partiality, and convict no one on a single witness.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as civil. The two-witness rule carried into the church's own discipline (Matthew 18:16; 1 Timothy 5:19), and the ban on bribes remains a standing test of any justice system.

Summary: The war laws: exemptions from service, the offer of peace before siege, protection of fruit trees, and limits on plunder and treatment of captives.
Commandment: Before battle, offer peace; exempt the newly married, the newly housed, and the fearful; spare fruit trees in a siege.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as civil. Even in war the Law set restraints — a striking limit for the ancient world, where siege warfare usually spared nothing. These laws bounded, but did not bless, every act of war.

Summary: The family laws: marriage protections, the divorce certificate, levirate marriage, and penalties for sexual offenses.
Commandment: Marry, divorce, and settle family disputes only by the Law's procedures, which protect the weaker party at each step.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as civil. Jesus appeals past the divorce certificate to creation: what God joined, man must not separate. The certificate restrained hasty divorce; it never made divorce God's design.

Summary: The servanthood laws: Hebrew servants freed after six years with provision, protections against cruelty, and the Jubilee release.
Commandment: Free a Hebrew servant after six years with generous provision, do not rule ruthlessly, and release all at Jubilee.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as civil. These laws regulated an ancient institution; they did not endorse it. Paul's letter to Philemon points past regulation toward brotherhood: Onesimus returns no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother.

Summary: Jesus' summary of the whole Law: love God with everything you are, and love your neighbor as yourself.
Commandment: Love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, and mind, and love your neighbor as yourself.
Application: Jesus says all the Law and the Prophets hang on these two. Every other command in this collection is an unfolding of one of them.

Command: The New Commandment: Love One Another
Summary: The command Jesus gave on the night before the cross: love one another as he has loved — a love measured by his own self-giving.
Commandment: Love one another just as Christ has loved you; let this love mark you as his disciples.
Application: The commandment is called new not because love was new, but because its measure is new: as I have loved you, even to laying down life for friends.

Summary: The risen Christ's charge to his church: go, make disciples of all nations, baptizing them and teaching them everything he commanded.
Commandment: Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything Christ commanded.
Application: The commission carries Christ's own authority — all authority in heaven and on earth — and his own promise: I am with you always, to the end of the age.

Summary: Jesus' opening proclamation: the kingdom of God is at hand, so turn from sin and trust the good news.
Commandment: Repent and believe the gospel, for the kingdom of God is at hand.
Application: Peter preaches the same command at Pentecost: repent and be baptized for the forgiveness of sins. Repentance and faith are the door into the kingdom, not works added to it.

Command: The Lord's Supper: Do This in Remembrance
Summary: The meal Christ instituted on the night he was betrayed: bread as his body, cup as the new covenant in his blood, eaten in remembrance until he comes.
Commandment: Eat the bread and drink the cup in remembrance of Christ, proclaiming his death until he comes.
Application: Paul delivers the same institution to Corinth and adds its rhythm: as often as you eat and drink, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes.

Command: Forgive as You Have Been Forgiven
Summary: The forgiveness command: forgive those who wrong you, as freely as God in Christ has forgiven you.
Commandment: Forgive those who sin against you, as your Father has forgiven you.
Application: Jesus ties our forgiveness to God's with unsettling directness, and the unforgiving servant shows what happens when a forgiven person refuses to forgive.

Summary: The judgment command: do not condemn others while blind to your own faults; judge with right judgment.
Commandment: Do not judge hypocritically; first take the plank from your own eye, then judge with right judgment.
Application: The command does not forbid all judgment — John 7:24 commands right judgment — but it forbids the hypocrite's judgment, which condemns in others what it excuses in itself.

Summary: The prayer Christ taught his disciples: a pattern for prayer that begins with God's name and kingdom before turning to daily needs.
Commandment: Pray like this: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name; your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as in heaven.
Application: The prayer is both a text to pray and a pattern to follow: God's glory first, then daily bread, forgiveness, and deliverance from evil.

Summary: The priority command: put God's kingdom and righteousness before food, clothing, and worry, and trust him for the rest.
Commandment: Seek first God's kingdom and his righteousness, and do not be anxious about food and clothing.
Application: The command reorders anxiety itself: worry is answered not by more provision but by a prior loyalty — the kingdom first, and all these things added.

Summary: The vine command: remain in Christ as a branch remains in the vine, or you can do nothing.
Commandment: Abide in me as I abide in you; apart from me you can do nothing.
Application: Abiding is not a feeling but a staying: keep his words, keep his commands, and let his life flow through you into fruit.

Summary: Paul's central command for Christian conduct: live by the Spirit's leading, and the works of the flesh lose their power.
Commandment: Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh; bear the Spirit's fruit instead.
Application: The fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control — is the character the Law aimed at but could not produce.

Summary: The burden-bearing command: carry the weight of a brother's failure, sorrow, and need, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
Commandment: Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
Application: Paul names this the law of Christ: strength exists to carry weakness, not to admire itself. The strong restore the fallen gently, watching themselves.

Summary: The gathering command: keep assembling with God's people for encouragement, especially as the Day draws near.
Commandment: Do not neglect meeting together, but encourage one another all the more as you see the Day approaching.
Application: The early church's pattern was daily fellowship, teaching, breaking of bread, and prayer. Gathering is not an optional extra but the place encouragement happens.

Summary: The authority command: submit to the governing powers, which God has instituted, and honor those in office.
Commandment: Submit to the governing authorities and honor those in office, for authority is instituted by God.
Application: Submission has its limit, which Scripture itself shows: where rulers command disobedience to God, believers obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). The command is submission, not worship of the state.

Summary: The household code: wives and husbands, children and parents, servants and masters — each with duties shaped by Christ's own pattern.
Commandment: Wives, submit to your husbands as to the Lord; husbands, love your wives as Christ loved the church; children, obey your parents; parents, do not provoke your children.
Application: The code's most radical stroke is its address to the powerful: husbands must love as Christ loved — giving himself up — and masters must remember they too have a Master in heaven.

Command: Pray Without Ceasing, Give Thanks in Everything
Summary: The unceasing-prayer command: rejoice always, pray continually, and give thanks in every circumstance.
Commandment: Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, and give thanks in all circumstances, for this is God's will for you in Christ Jesus.
Application: Thanksgiving in all circumstances is not denial of suffering but trust inside it — the peace of God guarding hearts that bring everything to him in prayer.

Summary: The stewardship command: hold fast the apostolic teaching, preach the word in season and out, and pass it to faithful people who will teach others.
Commandment: Preach the word in season and out of season, hold fast the pattern of sound words, and entrust it to faithful people who will teach others also.
Application: The teaching is a deposit to be guarded, not an invention to be improved. Each generation receives it, keeps it, and hands it on intact.

Command: Pure Religion: Care for Widows and Orphans
Summary: The pure-religion command: true devotion shows itself in visiting orphans and widows in their affliction and keeping unstained by the world.
Commandment: Visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and keep yourself unstained from the world.
Application: James makes care for the defenseless the test of real religion, not its decoration. Paul's instructions to Timothy organize that care in the church, honoring widows who are truly widows.

Summary: The impartiality command: do not favor the rich over the poor in the assembly or in judgment, for God shows no partiality.
Commandment: Do not show favoritism: treat the poor man in shabby clothes with the same honor as the rich man in fine clothes.
Application: James calls favoritism sin, plainly: it judges with evil thoughts and breaks the royal law of loving your neighbor. In Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female.

Command: Work Quietly and Provide for Your Household
Summary: The work command: earn your own living quietly, provide for your household, and do not live as a burden on others.
Commandment: Work quietly, earn your own living, and provide for your own household; if anyone will not work, neither shall he eat.
Application: Work is given dignity here: honest labor supports a family, funds generosity, and silences busybodies. Refusing to provide for one's own household is called a denial of the faith.

Summary: The tradition that the Torah contains 613 commandments — 248 positive and 365 negative — first systematized by medieval rabbis, not stated anywhere in Scripture itself.
Commandment: The Torah's commandments are traditionally counted as 613 in total.
Application: Scripture never gives a count of its own commandments; the 613 figure comes from rabbinic tradition (traced to Rabbi Simlai and codified by Maimonides), and different rabbinic lists disagree on details. It is a study aid, not a biblical census. Christians also differ on how the Mosaic law applies today — fulfilled in Christ, yet its moral substance enduring — which is why this collection treats the traditional moral/ceremonial/civil division as traditional, not as Scripture's own. A full 613-entry draft is a separate future decision, not attempted here.
